newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Petronas hits pay-dirt.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Petronas hits pay-dirt.

text.p: Malaysian state-oil company Petronas hit pay-dirt with its US$1.5 billion three-tranche global bond, Asian bankers said Thursday.
"The reception was very strong following roadshows in Asia, Europe and the U.S.," said Steve Roberts, managing director at Salomon Brothers, one of the deal's lead managers.
"I expect the pricing to be very tight and inside trading levels of the last issue," he added.
Petroliam Nasional launched the three bonds during London's afternoon session on Wednesday via lead managers Salomon Brothers and CS First Boston.
The bonds are set to price later today.
Tranche one is a US$600 million five-year bond that will be priced to yield 38-40 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
The US$600 million tranche two matures in 10 years and will be priced to yield 57-59 basis points over Treasuries.
Tranche three was a late entry to the field -- a US$300 million 30-year bond that will be priced to yield about 85 basis points over the benchmark.
"I think it will be a good deal, the pricing seems right, and I expect it will go well," remarked a syndicate manager at a European bank in Hong Kong.

Petronas launched a two-tranche bond issue in August 1995 that paid 69 basis points over Treasuries for the 10-year paper and 86 basis points over for the 20-year bond, much wider spreads than indicated on the latest issue.
Asian bankers said they expect most of the paper to place outside Asia, largely because of the long maturities.
They said almost all of the 30-year is likely to go to the U.S., where there is a huge institutional investor base happy to take very long-dated paper.
Some said distribution desks in Asia are not set up to handle this type of transaction, since most of the paper that flows in the region is shorter-term and floating rate.
"There are so few transactions of that nature out here that sales people just haven't developed an interest or a group of investors that might buy," said a Hong Kong banker.
But others said they expect a decent Asian response.
"We've seen a good cross section of where the paper has gone," said a participant in the deal, adding "we expect to sell some here, some in Europe and some in the States, which is usual for us."
Salomon's Roberts said the success of the issue reflected support for Malaysia generally and Petronas specifically.
"There is strong support for Malaysia, for its policies and economic performance, as well as for the economic fundamentals of Petronas," he said.
Petronas in September reported a record net profit of 6.76 billion ringgit (US$2.6 billion) for the financial year ended March 31, 1996, an increase of 48.3 percent.
Because Malaysia has not issued in its own name for a number of years, Petronas has been the most liquid Malaysian credit, Roberts said.
"The advantage that Petronas offers is that it has now established a proprietary yield curve from five to 30 years with great liquidity throughout," he said.
